query: For HfNbTaTiZr refractory high-entropy alloy, stress–strain behavior, thermal expansion, and elastic behavior at elevated temperatures remain insufficiently understood. What testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain these responses? Define a controlled comparison, the observations predicted relative to a baseline state, the temperature and response limits within which the hypothesis should hold, supporting prior evidence, and a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: In the single‐phase BCC HfNbTaTiZr refractory HEA, the inherent lattice distortions arising from the atomic size mismatch create local stress fields that at room temperature resist deformation. When heated into an elevated temperature regime (e.g. 600–900 °C) but before any microstructural degradation occurs, thermally induced atomic vibrations partially relax these local distortions and lower the barriers for activating multiple slip systems. This temperature‐dependent relaxation accounts for the observed decreases in yield strength and elastic modulus as well as non-linear thermal expansion behavior.
generation.material_initial_state: Homogenized, single‐phase BCC HfNbTaTiZr alloy with pronounced lattice distortions from atomic size mismatch.
generation.intervention: Subject the alloy to controlled mechanical testing (stress–strain) and thermal expansion measurements at a series of elevated temperatures (e.g., 600, 750, and 900 °C) while using in situ characterization (e.g., high‐temperature XRD and TEM) to monitor changes in lattice parameters and slip system activity.
generation.conditions: Temperature range below the onset of microstructural degradation or phase transformation (approximately 600–900 °C) and comparable strain rate conditions to ensure thermally activated mechanisms dominate.
generation.structural_mediator: Local lattice distortions (atomic-scale misfits) that induce heterogeneous internal stress fields, which relax with temperature.
generation.mechanism: Elevated temperatures increase the amplitude of atomic vibrations, thereby reducing the effective intensity of local lattice distortions. This relaxation lowers the yield barrier and modulus, facilitates the activation of multiple {110} or non-traditional slip systems, and causes a non-linear increase in the lattice spacing (thermal expansion), leading to improved ductility and modified elastic responses.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to room temperature baseline, the alloy will exhibit: (a) decreased yield strength and Young’s modulus, (b) an increase in ductility via activation of multiple slip systems as confirmed by in situ TEM or diffraction, and (c) a non-linear, enhanced thermal expansion coefficient in the 600–900 °C range.
generation.baseline: Mechanical and thermal responses measured at room temperature, where local lattice distortions are fully intact and deformation is mainly resisted by a high internal stress field.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is expected to hold in the absence of microstructural degradation (e.g. precipitation, phase transitions) – specifically within the temperature window of roughly 600–900 °C and under moderate strain rates where thermal activation predominates over dynamic recrystallization or diffusion-driven transformations.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative extent of property changes (e.g., percentage decrease in yield strength or modulus) is uncertain without further experimental calibration, and competing mechanisms (e.g. incipient dislocation nucleation anomalies) might also contribute.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform high-temperature in situ tensile tests and thermal expansion measurements on HfNbTaTiZr samples across the 600–900 °C range. Simultaneously, use high-temperature XRD and TEM to track changes in lattice parameters and identify active slip systems. Compare these observations to room temperature benchmarks.
measurements: Yield strength and Young’s modulus at multiple temperatures
Lattice parameter changes via high-temperature XRD
Slip system activation and dislocation behavior via TEM or diffraction techniques
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the elevated temperature tests do not show a correlated decrease in elastic modulus/yield strength accompanied by evidence of relaxed lattice distortions (e.g., unchanged local lattice strain and activation of additional slip systems), or if significant microstructural transformations occur within the tested temperature window that dominate the mechanical behavior, then the hypothesis is falsified.

Microstructural Degradation of the AlMo0.5NbTa0.5TiZr Refractory Metal High-Entropy Superalloy at Elevated Temperatures

Abstract: AbstractRefractory metal high-entropy superalloys (RSA), which possess a nanoscale microstructure of B2 and bcc phases, have been developed to offer high temperature capabilities beyond conventional Ni-based alloys. Despite showing a number of excellent attributes, to date there has been little consideration of their microstructural stability, which is an essential feature of any material employed in high temperature service. Here, the stability of the exemplar RSA AlMo0.5NbTa0.5TiZr is studied following 1000 h exposures at 1200, 1000 and 800 °C. Crucially, the initial nanoscale cuboidal B2 + bcc microstructure was found to be unstable following the thermal exposures. Extensive intragranular precipitation of a hexagonal Al-Zr-rich intermetallic occurred at all temperatures and, where present, the bcc and B2 phases had coarsened and changed morphology. Microstructure and Mechanical Properties of Intergranular Boride Precipitation-Toughened HfMoNbTaTiZr Refractory High-Entropy Alloy

Abstract: AbstractTo develop strong refractory high-entropy alloys for use at elevated temperatures as well as to overcome grain-boundary brittleness, an equimolar HfMoNbTaTiZr alloy was prepared, and a minor amount of boron (0.1 at.%) was added into the alloy. The microstructures of the alloys were characterized, and their macro-to-microscale mechanical properties were measured. The microstructural observations indicated that the matrices of both the alloys were composed of a body-centered cubic solid-solution structure, and the added boron induced the precipitation of hexagonal close-packed borides (most likely the (Hf, Zr)B2) at the grain boundaries. The modulus and hardness of differently oriented grains were about equivalent, suggesting a diminished anisotropy, and many small slips occurred on multiple {110} planes. While the hardness of the matrix was not increased, the intergranular precipitation of the borides markedly raised the hardness of the grain boundaries.
